description: We’re ktech team . Our hobbies are surviving 52°C summers, breathing dust for free, and pretending we understand satellites. Now we’re going to actually understand them and try to  win this thing, inshallah (the real kind, not the “I’ll send it tomorrow” kind).
summary: Weather Witness turns 45 years of NASA daily weather data into something anyone can read: two childhoods in the same city, side by side. Pick any of 6,266 cities, or any point on Earth, and two birth years. The site compares the first ten years of each life: unusually hot days, warm nights, rain, humidity, dust and the ground. Every number goes through a Mann-Kendall trend test with Sen’s slope and is stamped “Real change” or “No clear change”, so people can tell a real trend from a few bad years. It answers the challenge’s four questions (what is changing, where, how much, and whether it is significant) in everyday words, for parents, outdoor workers, farmers and teachers. In Kuwait City, a child born in 2015 gets 57 more unusually warm nights a year than one born in 1981
details:
What it does
Weather Witness is a free website that shows how the weather where you live has changed, in words anyone can read. You pick any of 6,266 cities, or any point on Earth, and two birth years, for example 1981 and 2015. The site puts the first ten years of each childhood side by side, “Then” and “Now”. Sticky notes say what changed, by how much, and whether the change is real. In Kuwait City, a child born in 2015 gets 57 more unusually warm nights a year than one born in 1981.

How it works
When you pick a city, the site pulls 45 years of daily NASA POWER data (1981–2025, over 16,000 days) live from NASA’s servers in about three seconds. A “What NASA sends us” button shows one raw day, so you can see what we translate.
From those days the site counts 18 everyday measures, such as unusually hot days, warm nights, heatwave days, rainy days, the longest dry spell, sticky days and perfect outdoor days. Each one is judged against the city’s own 1981–2010 normal. Every measure goes through a Mann-Kendall trend test (with the Hamed-Rao correction) and Sen’s slope, and gets a “Real change” or “No clear change” stamp.
“More evidence” adds NASA GPM satellite rain, CERES dust and haze, and MERRA-2 data on the ground. “Two futures” continues each real trend to a child born in 2030, 2040 or 2050, once at the same pace and once at half the pace. It is labelled as a what-if, not a forecast.

Benefits and intended impact
NASA’s data mostly sits unread. Weather Witness turns it into evidence that a parent, teacher, outdoor worker, farmer or city planner can understand in a minute. Visitors choose who they are, and the site shows the measures that matter for that life. We want people to see that heat is real, local and unequal (Kuwait City against London), and that it can still slow down.

Tools
TypeScript and React, built with Vite, served from GitHub Pages and deployed by GitHub Actions. The statistics are written in TypeScript and checked by 123 automatic tests (Vitest) against a Python reference (NumPy, pandas, SciPy, pymannkendall). FFmpeg and Pillow were used for the demo video. No special hardware is needed: it runs in any phone or laptop browser, with no login. Code: https://github.com/catoooos21/Weather-Witness

What makes it creative
Instead of leading with charts, it tells the data as two childhoods in a scrapbook. It treats NASA as a witness: every claim has to pass a statistical test before we call it real.

What we considered
Honesty: we show “No clear change” results too. The page states the limits: MERRA-2 is a model fed by observations, one grid square of about 50 km stands for a whole city, and rain is less certain than temperature.
Fairness: each city is compared with its own normal, not with one global threshold.
Access: plain English, built for phones, free and with no account, so anyone can use it.
